item.title: Google Search Console: Getting Started and the Metrics That Matter (2026)
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
Google Search Console is the closest thing most UK businesses have to a direct line into how Google sees their website. It is free, it is first-party data, and it answers the questions that guesswork cannot: which queries you appear for, which pages actually get clicked, what is indexed, and where the site is failing technically.

This guide covers the core setup steps to get started properly, the reports you should live in week to week, and the metrics that matter for both classic SEO and Generative Engine Optimisation (GEO) — because what Google indexes is still the raw material AI Overviews and other generative answers draw from.

Key GLC Insight:

Search Console is not a vanity dashboard. Treat clicks, impressions, coverage and page experience as a single operating system: if a page is not valid in the index, it cannot rank — and it is far less likely to be cited in AI-generated answers.

What Google Search Console is — and what it is not

Search Console reports how Google Search interacted with your property. It is not Google Analytics. Analytics tells you what people did after they arrived. Search Console tells you what happened in the search results before they clicked — and whether Google could crawl and index the page at all.

Use both. Search Console for discovery and technical health; Analytics (or your equivalent) for on-site behaviour and conversions. Linking the two accounts lets you see query and landing-page data in Analytics without treating either tool as a substitute for the other.

Getting started: the core setup

1. Choose the right property type

A Domain property covers every subdomain and protocol (http, https, www and non-www) once you verify via DNS. A URL prefix property covers only the exact prefix you verify — for example https://www.example.co.uk/.

For most businesses, Domain is the cleaner long-term choice: one property, one set of reports, fewer gaps when you add a staging subdomain or migrate to HTTPS. If you already have prefix properties, you can keep them and add a Domain property alongside.

2. Verify ownership

DNS TXT (or CNAME) is the most robust method for a Domain property. URL prefix properties can also verify with a HTML file upload, a meta tag, or via Google Analytics / Google Tag Manager if those snippets are already on every page.

Complete verification before you start reading reports. Unverified access is limited, and you cannot submit sitemaps or inspect URLs as the owner.

3. Submit an XML sitemap

Go to Indexing → Sitemaps and submit the sitemap URL WordPress (or your SEO plugin) already generates — typically /sitemap_index.xml or /sitemap.xml. Search Console does not guarantee indexing, but a clean sitemap is still the fastest way to tell Google which URLs you consider canonical.

Check the sitemap status after 24–48 hours. “Couldn’t fetch” almost always means a robots.txt block, a 404, or a plugin serving the file with the wrong content type.

4. Confirm robots.txt and canonicals are not fighting you

Open Settings → robots.txt (or fetch the live file) and make sure you are not disallowing CSS, JS or important template paths. Then spot-check a handful of money pages with the URL Inspection tool: Google’s chosen canonical should match the URL you want to rank.

5. Set users and email alerts

Add the people who actually need access — owner, full user or restricted — and turn on email notifications for manual actions, security issues and data anomalies. Search Console is most valuable when someone notices a crawl collapse the same week it happens, not three months later in a quarterly review.

The reports that matter first

You do not need every report on day one. Start with these four, then add Links and Experience once the basics are stable.

Performance (Search results)

This is the commercial report. Filter by search type (Web is the default), date range, query, page, country, device and search appearance. For UK businesses, pin Country to United Kingdom unless you genuinely serve other markets — mixed-country totals hide local problems.

Pages (Indexing)

Formerly “Coverage”. It splits URLs into why they are indexed or why they are not: not found, redirect, excluded by ‘noindex’, crawled – currently not indexed, duplicate without user-selected canonical, and so on. This is where technical SEO either holds or quietly fails.

URL Inspection

Use this for individual pages after a publish, a redesign or a migration. Request indexing only for URLs that are already live, canonical and internally linked — it is a nudge, not a queue-jump for an entire site.

Experience and enhancements

Core Web Vitals, HTTPS and (where relevant) rich result types such as FAQ, Product or Article. Enhancements tell you whether structured data is valid enough for extra search features — which also helps machines parse your content for generative answers.

The metrics to measure

Four numbers sit at the top of Performance. Read them as a set, never in isolation.

  • Impressions: how often a link to your property appeared in search results. Rising impressions with flat clicks usually means you are visible for queries you have not yet earned (or you are stuck on page two).
  • Clicks: how often someone followed that link. This is your search traffic, not your branded homepage visits from typing the URL.
  • Average CTR: clicks divided by impressions. Title, meta description, sitelinks and rich results all move this. A high position with a weak CTR is almost always a snippet problem, not a ranking problem.
  • Average position: the mean ranking of your URLs for the filtered queries. It is a blended number — useful for trend, dangerous as a KPI on its own because one viral branded query can flatter the whole site.

How to slice the data so it is useful

  • Queries: separate branded vs non-branded. Brand terms should convert; non-brand is where SEO and GEO work shows up.
  • Pages: find landing pages with impressions but weak CTR, and pages with clicks but no conversions in Analytics — those are two different fixes.
  • Devices: mobile vs desktop. If mobile CTR or Core Web Vitals lag, that is where Google (and most users) will feel it first.
  • Dates: compare 28 days vs the previous 28, then 3 months vs 3 months, so you do not overreact to a single algorithm week.
  • Search appearance: isolate AI Overviews, rich results or Discover where the report is available, so you can see how generative surfaces change click behaviour even when impressions hold.

Indexing metrics you should actually track

  • Valid pages: should trend with the number of URLs you intentionally publish — not with parameter junk or thin archives.
  • Error / not found / server error: treat as incidents. A spike after a plugin update or host change is a crawl emergency.
  • Crawled – currently not indexed: quality and consolidation signal. If important service pages sit here, they need stronger internal links, clearer purpose, or less duplication.
  • Excluded by noindex / canonical: confirm these are deliberate (thank-you pages, filters, paginated leftovers), not accidental.

Experience metrics

Watch the share of URLs that are “good” for Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift, split by mobile and desktop. You do not need a perfect Lighthouse score on a staging URL — you need field data in Search Console to stay in the “good” bucket for the URLs that already attract impressions.

Why this matters for GEO as well as SEO

Generative answers still depend on pages Google can fetch, understand and trust. If Search Console shows a service page as excluded, duplicate or “crawled – not indexed”, that page is a poor candidate for citation in AI Overviews, ChatGPT-style answers that draw on the open web, or any engine that starts from a search index.

Practically, GEO work on a UK site still starts here: valid indexation, a sitemap Google accepts, queries you already almost rank for, and snippets that state a clear answer. Structured data and extractable headings help machines quote you — but only after the URL is in the index.

A simple 30-day operating rhythm

  1. Weekly: Performance 7-day vs previous 7-day (clicks, impressions, CTR). Open Pages for new errors. Inspect any URL you published or redirected.
  2. Fortnightly: Query report — pick five non-brand queries in positions 4–15 and improve the matching page (title, H1, first paragraph, internal links).
  3. Monthly: Indexing totals, sitemap status, Core Web Vitals, and a branded vs non-branded split so you can see whether growth is real demand or just people searching your name.

Export the Performance table occasionally. Search Console’s on-screen view is capped; a spreadsheet lets you catch long-tail queries that never appear in the first 1,000 rows of the UI.

Ready to put Search Console to work?

Setup is the easy part. The advantage comes from reading the reports against your commercial pages — service landing pages, location pages and guides — and fixing what Google is already telling you.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to discuss Search Console setup, technical SEO, GEO visibility and a measurement plan that fits your site.

item.title: Claude’s AI Watermark: Why It Matters If You Have Outsourced Your Content
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic has started marking Claude’s output in a way you cannot see. From August 2026, supported Claude models weave a statistical watermark into generated text, and attach cryptographically signed provenance metadata to supported image files. The trigger is the EU AI Act’s transparency rules — but Anthropic is applying the marks worldwide because it cannot yet scope them by region.

That is a bigger moment than another product changelog. A large share of businesses have quietly moved from “AI as a drafting assistant” to “AI as the content department”. If your publishing model is paste, publish and hope, a machine-readable mark — and a wave of detectors that will follow — changes the risk profile of that habit. Not because Google has banned AI. It has not. Because the web is about to get much better at asking whether anyone actually did the work.

Key GLC Insight:

Google still judges pages on helpfulness, not on whether a model touched the draft. The ranking risk is unmeasured, interchangeable content — and the operational risk is treating cheap AI-detector scores as gospel when a grammar pass can look “synthetic” and a watermark can miss a light edit.

What Claude’s watermark actually is

It is not a faint logo behind the paragraph. Anthropic uses a version of Google DeepMind’s SynthID-Text approach: when the model chooses among several equally good next words, it uses a keyed pattern instead of an arbitrary random draw. Over a long passage those choices add up to a signal. A reader cannot see it. There are no hidden characters and no extra tokens — so it does not cost more to run.

Two other facts matter for publishers:

  • The mark is about Claude’s involvement, not about you. Anthropic says it cannot be traced to a person, organisation or chat.
  • A detected mark is a probability, not a courtroom stamp. It cannot tell “Claude wrote this” from “Claude heavily edited this”. Short passages, tightly factual sentences and code leave less room for the watermark to attach.

For images, the mechanism is different: signed C2PA content credentials in the file metadata — a note that Claude created or processed the file, not a pattern baked into the pixels.

Anthropic has said a detection API is coming. Other major model providers signed the same EU Code of Practice. Expect a messy year of overlapping watermarks, not a single “AI or not” light on every page.

Why this is significant if you have outsourced writing to a model

Until now, “was this written by AI?” lived in the land of vibes and third-party classifiers. Those tools guess from style — favourite constructions, evenly polished sentences, a suspiciously calm vocabulary. Claude’s watermark is a different class of evidence: it is applied at generation time by the model provider, with a key.

If your content pipeline is “prompt → paste into WordPress → rank”, you have been betting that nobody could prove the shortcut, and that Google would not care. The second half of that bet can still be true. The first half is getting weaker.

This is significant for three practical reasons:

  • Trust becomes inspectable. Clients, journalists, universities and platforms will eventually have a button. “We used AI for research” is a grown-up answer. “We published 80 location pages nobody in the business could defend” will not be.
  • GEO cares about citable sources. Generative engines prefer pages they can treat as a source, not another remix of the same model sludge. If the open web is increasingly labelled as processed by a frontier model, undifferentiated AI blogs become even less useful to quote.
  • Editing is not laundering. Anthropic is clear that light edits often leave the watermark in place. A full rewrite, where every word is replaced, can remove it — at which point you have done the work the model was supposed to skip.

Google does not ban AI. It bans the business model of slop

Google’s Search Central guidance has been consistent since 2023: using automation, including AI, to generate content primarily to manipulate rankings is spam. Using AI to help produce useful, original, people-first pages is not against the guidelines. AI does not get a ranking bonus. It is just content. If it demonstrates experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust — and it actually helps the searcher — it can do well. If it is interchangeable filler, it will not, whether a human or a model typed it.

Be realistic about what that means in 2026:

  • There is still no public “Claude watermark ranking factor”. Do not rewrite your strategy around a leak that has not happened.
  • There is a sitewide quality problem when dozens of thin, lookalike pages exist mainly to capture queries. Helpful-content thinking now sits inside core ranking, not as a one-off update you can wait out.
  • AI Overviews and other generative answers reduce clicks on generic explainers. Pages that only restate what a model already knows are the first to become invisible — watermark or not.
  • If search engines, browsers or social platforms start surfacing provenance at scale, unlabelled mass generation becomes a reputation issue even when it is not a hard penalty.

The honest ranking impact is this: AI will not sink a page that a real specialist would be proud to put their name on. Relying solely on AI to industrialise average articles will look more and more like the scaled, unoriginal content Google has been trying to demote for years. The watermark just makes the industrialisation easier to talk about.

Measure the work. Do not worship a detector score

If you take one operational lesson from this, make it measurement — of outcomes, not of “% human”.

Track whether pages earn impressions and clicks in Search Console, whether they pick up non-brand queries, whether they are valid in the index, and whether people who land actually enquire. For GEO, track whether your brand is cited in AI answers for the questions you care about. Those numbers tell you if the content is doing a job.

An AI-detector percentage does not. Treat it as a noisy secondary signal at best.

Why a grammar check can get you falsely marked as AI

Here is the part many teams will get wrong. They will run every draft through Grammarly, Hemingway or Claude-as-proofreader, then panic when Originality.ai, GPTZero or a CMS plugin screams “AI generated”.

Those classifiers are not reading Anthropic’s key. They are scoring how the text looks: uniform sentence length, tidy transitions, low burstiness, stock phrases models overuse. A human who writes in a second language, a solicitor who prefers plain structured English, or a marketer who has had every comma professionally corrected can trip the same heuristics.

Anthropic’s own explanation cuts the other way for true watermarks: if you hand Claude a piece of writing and ask it to fix only grammar and punctuation, almost every word is still yours. The watermark has very little to attach to and may not register. So you can have a page that is fully human in origin, grammatically polished, and still flagged by a consumer detector — while a lightly Claude-edited page might carry a provider watermark that a style-based tool never sees.

That mismatch is why “we got 12% AI on the checker, so we are safe / we are doomed” is not a strategy. False positives punish careful editors. False negatives reassure people who published 4,000 words of unreviewed model output.

A grown-up way to use AI after watermarks

  • Start from something only you know: a job completed, a process, a local constraint, a dataset, a point of view. If the page could have been written by any model with a homepage URL, it is already weak for SEO and GEO.
  • Use models for structure and challenge, not for the finished article. Outline, counter-arguments, FAQs — then write or heavily rewrite in a voice you would stand behind on a sales call.
  • Keep an editorial record. Who briefed it, who checked facts, what was unique. When a client or a platform asks, you will have an answer that is not a detector screenshot.
  • Measure weekly: Search Console queries and pages, indexing errors, on-site conversions, and a handful of AI-answer spot checks for your money terms.
  • Do not buy “humaniser” tools as a ranking strategy. If the only value you add is scrambling tokens until a watermark or a classifier goes quiet, you have admitted the page had nothing to say.

What to do next

Claude’s watermark will not, by itself, decide your rankings tomorrow morning. It is a transparency layer arriving at the same time as generative search, EU rules and a public fatigue with AI slop. That combination is the significance.

If your content still needs a human who has done the work — and you can prove it with Search Console, citations and enquiries — you can keep using AI as a tool. If the tool is the work, this is the moment to change the process, not to hunt for a better spinner.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review your content process, Search Console measurement and GEO visibility — including how to use AI without building a site of unreviewable pages.

Google’s August 2026 Core Update Is Rolling Out — Here’s What Actually Matters
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
Google began rolling out its August 2026 core update on 26 August. If you’ve noticed your traffic wobbling this week, or you’re just wondering whether now’s a bad time to touch your website, this is why — and here’s what’s actually worth doing about it.

Key GLC Insight:

A core update is Google raising the bar for the whole index, not a penalty on your business. The pages that hold are the ones a visitor couldn’t get from any other local competitor — and rewriting them mid-rollout just makes it impossible to tell what actually worked.

What actually happened

Core updates are Google periodically re-tuning how it judges the whole index, not a punishment aimed at any one site. This one arrived after a stretch of unconfirmed volatility through late July and early August that had a lot of site owners nervously refreshing Search Console before Google had even confirmed anything was happening. The confirmed update itself started on the 26th, and — like most core updates — it’ll likely take one to three weeks to fully roll out.

The pattern several SEO trackers are reporting is a familiar one, just sharper than before: pages that mostly restate what’s already ranking elsewhere are losing ground, while pages built on something Google can’t get anywhere else — original data, first-hand experience, a genuinely local answer — are holding up or gaining. That’s not a new rule. It’s the same “helpful content” direction Google’s been pushing for a couple of years now, tightened another notch.

What this means for your business

If you run a small business website, you probably don’t have hundreds of thin, interchangeable pages to worry about — but the underlying test still applies to whatever you do have. Ask honestly: if your service page disappeared tomorrow, would a visitor notice anything missing that they couldn’t get from any other local competitor’s site? Pages that answer yes to that — genuine photos of your actual work, specific detail about how you do things, real local knowledge — tend to be the ones that hold steady through updates like this.

This is also exactly the kind of moment where reactive panic does more damage than the update itself. Rewriting pages mid-rollout means you’ll never know whether a recovery was your change or the algorithm settling back down.

What to check in Search Console this week

You don’t need to do anything drastic right now, but it is worth a quick, calm look:

  • Compare this week’s clicks and impressions with the week before 26 August, not with last month — you want a clean before/after.
  • Note which pages moved, not just whether overall traffic moved. A handful of pages dropping is a very different situation to a sitewide fall.
  • Fix anything genuinely broken regardless of the update — dead links, missing pages, titles nobody’s clicking — since those are worth fixing either way.

If you haven’t got Search Console properly set up to actually see this, GLC’s guide to getting started and the metrics that actually matter is worth a read before you draw any conclusions from this update.

What not to do yet

Google’s own guidance is to wait a full week after a core update completes — not after it starts — before analysing your Search Console data properly. On a rollout that could run two to three weeks, that means giving it real time before making big changes. Don’t rewrite content based on day-three panic. Do keep an eye on it, and do get in touch if a genuine, sustained drop shows up rather than normal noise.

GLC looked at Google’s previous core update from December 2025 in a similar way at the time — see how that one played out.

Frequently asked questions

How long does a Google core update take to finish?

Recent core updates have typically taken one to three weeks to fully roll out, though Google doesn’t publish an exact schedule or duration in advance.

How do I know if my site was actually affected?

Compare Search Console clicks and impressions for the week before the update started against a recent week, once the rollout has finished and settled — not mid-rollout, when the numbers are still moving around.

Should I change my website while a core update is rolling out?

Generally, no — wait until the update completes and the data settles before making changes, so you can tell whether a drop was the update or something else on your site.

Where this leaves you

A core update isn’t a verdict on your business — it’s Google re-sorting the whole index against a slightly higher bar. If your site does something a visitor genuinely couldn’t get anywhere else, that’s usually enough to hold up through updates like this one. If reading this has made you wonder whether your own site would pass that test, that’s exactly the kind of thing a quick conversation sorts out — and it’s worth knowing GLC’s SEO & GEO service is built around practical changes rather than a report you’ll never read.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review your Search Console data, check whether a drop is the update or something else, and decide what — if anything — is worth changing once the rollout settles.

item.title: AI Shopping Agents Just Got Real — Is Your Website Ready?
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
On 2 September, Anthropic (the company behind the Claude AI models) released something called “Commerce Agents” — free, open-source blueprints that let any developer build an AI agent that can browse product catalogues, compare prices, fill a shopping cart, and hand it off for checkout. A day later, coverage from MarkTechPost confirmed the code works across retail, travel, telecoms and entertainment, and runs on nothing more exotic than a standard developer laptop and an API key.

If that sounds like something only Amazon-sized retailers need to think about, I’d have said the same a year ago. But the direction of travel matters more than the release itself, and it’s worth five minutes of a busy owner’s time to understand why.

Key GLC Insight:

You don’t need to build an AI shopping agent. You need a site an agent can actually read — real names, prices and stock in the HTML, not buried in a PDF or a graphic. If a machine cannot parse what you sell, you will not be in the basket it builds.

What Anthropic actually announced

The blueprint ships two types of agent. A “shopping agent” does the browsing on a customer’s behalf — searching catalogues, comparing options, building a basket. A “merchant agent” sits on the business side, handling things like inventory and pricing logic. Notably, Anthropic left payments and checkout out of it entirely — no money moves through Anthropic’s systems, and transactions still run through a retailer’s existing payment setup (Visa, Mastercard, whatever you already use). According to Anthropic’s own reporting, cited by PYMNTS, retailers piloting the agents saw carts grow up to 35% larger and shoppers were 60% more likely to complete a purchase — figures worth treating as an early, self-reported signal rather than a guarantee, but a signal all the same.

This isn’t a finished product a small business can switch on tomorrow — it’s scaffolding aimed at developers. But it’s the clearest evidence yet that the big AI labs expect AI agents doing the “browsing” and “comparing” part of shopping to become normal, not niche.

What this means if you’re not a big retailer

You don’t need to build an AI agent to be affected by this. The more relevant question is: if an AI agent — a customer’s ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini assistant — goes looking on a customer’s behalf, can it actually understand your website?

Agents (and the AI Overviews and AI Mode features already built into Google) work by reading a page’s actual content and structured data, not by “seeing” a page the way a person does. A site with clear product information, accurate prices, working stock status, and clean underlying code is legible to an agent. A site that’s all images and vague copy, or one where prices live only in a PDF price list, effectively doesn’t exist to it.

This is a continuation of a trend GLC has covered before with GEO (generative engine optimisation) — it’s the same fundamentals, applied to a slightly different use case.

What to actually check on your own site

A few concrete things worth checking now, none of which require an AI agent to exist yet:

  • Product and service pages have real text, not just images — names, prices, availability, and specifics, in HTML that can be read, not baked into a graphic.
  • Structured data (schema markup) is in place for products, services, and pricing, so search engines and agents alike can parse what you’re selling without guesswork.
  • Prices and stock are accurate and current — an agent (or a person) landing on an out-of-date price is a trust problem, not just an SEO one.
  • Checkout and contact paths still work simply for a human who lands after an AI-assisted search, since Anthropic’s approach — and the wider industry data on in-chat checkout underperforming — both point to purchases still finishing on the business’s own site.

Frequently asked questions

What is an AI shopping agent?

Software that browses websites, compares products or services, and builds a shopping basket on a person’s behalf — using an AI model like Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini to do the “looking around” part a person would normally do themselves.

Do AI agents actually buy from small business websites yet?

Not routinely, and Anthropic’s own release deliberately leaves payment and checkout out of it. What’s changing is the browsing and comparing stage — which makes how clearly your site presents information more important, not less.

Do I need structured data for AI shopping agents to find me?

It helps considerably. Structured data (schema markup) is the clearest way to tell an AI system exactly what you sell, for how much, and whether it’s in stock, rather than leaving it to interpret images or loosely worded copy.

Is this only relevant to online shops?

No — the same legibility principle applies to any small business site, whether you’re selling products, taking bookings, or just want an AI-generated answer to accurately describe your services and prices.

Where GLC fits in

None of this means overhauling your website overnight. It means the businesses whose sites are clean, accurately structured, and easy to parse — by people and by AI systems alike — are the ones best placed as this shift continues. That’s exactly the groundwork covered in GLC’s SEO & GEO audits, and it’s built in from the start on every site we design (see website design and development).

If you’re not sure where your own site stands, it’s worth reading our earlier guide on optimising your website for GEO, or, for an easier first step, take up GLC’s free, no-obligation website design offer — a good excuse to get a second pair of eyes on how your site actually reads, to a person and to a machine.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review whether your product and service pages are actually readable to search engines and AI agents — and what to fix first.

item.title: Chrome Now Updates Every Two Weeks — Here’s What That Means For Your Website
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
From 8 September 2026, Google Chrome is switching from a monthly release schedule to a new version every fortnight. Chrome 153 is the first release under the new cadence, with Chrome 154 following just fourteen days later on 22 September. If you run a website, or pay someone to run one for you, that’s worth two minutes of your attention — not because it’s alarming, but because “the browser most of your visitors use” just started changing twice as fast as it used to.

Key GLC Insight:

Chrome speeding up is not the threat. An unwatched booking widget, an old plugin or a third-party script nobody owns is. Two-week releases just shrink the window before a visitor finds the problem instead of you.

What’s actually changing

Chrome has shipped a new major version roughly every four weeks for years, with smaller security patches slotted in between. From Chrome 153 onward, that four-week cycle becomes two weeks, across desktop, Android and iOS. Google says the point is to get both new features and security fixes to users faster, using more automated testing to keep the shorter cycle stable. Businesses that need a slower, more predictable pace can enrol managed devices in Chrome’s “Extended Stable” channel, which keeps the old eight-week rhythm — but that’s an IT department opt-in, not something that happens by default.

Why Google is doing this

The short version: faster patching means a smaller window between a security flaw being found and a fix reaching everyone’s browser. Chrome has already been shipping weekly security patches for a while; this extends the same logic to full version releases. It’s a sensible move for user safety, and it’s not really optional for anyone — Chrome still auto-updates in the background for the vast majority of visitors to your site.

What this means for your business

For most small business websites, the honest answer is: probably nothing breaks. Chrome’s team tests heavily for backward compatibility, and a well-built, actively maintained site will sail through most releases without anyone noticing. The risk isn’t Chrome itself — it’s everything bolted onto your site that nobody’s looked at in a while: an old booking widget, a chat plugin last updated in 2023, a theme customisation done by a freelancer who’s since moved on, or a script pulling data from a third-party service that’s also changing on its own schedule.

A site like that used to have roughly a month between Chrome releases to quietly develop a problem before anyone noticed. Now it has two weeks. That doesn’t mean panic-testing your site every fortnight — it means the cost of an unmaintained site quietly going stale has gone up slightly, and it’s worth knowing whether yours falls into that category.

Signs your website might be at risk

A few practical things worth checking, or asking whoever manages your site about:

  • When was your website theme, plugins or booking/e-commerce integrations last updated?
  • Does anyone actually check your site in a current browser on a regular basis, or only when a customer complains?
  • Do you have backups and basic monitoring in place, so a browser-related issue gets caught and fixed quickly rather than sitting there costing you enquiries?

If you don’t know the answers, that’s not a crisis — it just means nobody really owns that job for your site right now.

How to stay ahead of it without becoming a browser-update-watcher

You don’t need to track Chrome’s release notes yourself — that’s genuinely not a good use of a business owner’s time. What’s worth having is a website that’s actively looked after: kept updated, checked periodically in current browsers, and backed up, so that if something does break after an update, it gets caught in days rather than found by a frustrated customer. Having run large commercial websites for years before starting GLC, this is the same principle that applies at any scale — the sites that cause problems are the ones nobody’s watching, not the ones on old software per se.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to test my website every two weeks now?

No — that’s more than most small businesses need. What matters is that someone checks your site periodically and keeps its software up to date, not that you personally track every Chrome release.

Will Chrome’s new update break my website?

Almost certainly not, if your site is actively maintained. The risk sits with old, unmaintained plugins, themes or third-party scripts rather than with Chrome itself.

What is Chrome Extended Stable, and do I need it?

It’s an eight-week release channel Google offers for managed business devices that want a slower, more predictable update pace. It’s an IT setup choice, not something that affects how your website behaves for visitors.

How do I know if my website is at risk?

Check when your theme, plugins and integrations were last updated, and whether anyone reviews your site regularly. If you’re not sure, it’s worth a quick look from someone who manages websites for a living.

The easy first step

None of this needs to be something you manage yourself. If reading this made you wonder when anyone last actually checked your website, GLC Web Solutions offers a free website design or refresh — no obligation to pay a thing if you’re not happy with it — as a low-pressure way to find out where your site actually stands. For businesses that would rather never think about this again, our website design and development service includes an ongoing managed option with regular reviews built in, so updates like Chrome’s new cycle are someone else’s job, not yours.

If you’re curious how AI-powered browsers fit into this same shift, we covered Comet, Atlas, Dia and Claude for Chrome in an earlier post.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to talk it through — straight answers, no sales script.

item.title: Google's August 2026 Spam Update Hit Rankings Harder Than Usual: Here's What It Means for Your Website
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
If your website's Google ranking took an unexpected dip in the last couple of weeks of August, you're not imagining it, and you're not alone. Google ran a spam update between 18 and 21 August 2026, and by most measures it shook up search results more than a typical update does. Here's what actually happened, and what it does (and doesn't) mean if you run a small business website.

Key GLC Insight:

A spam update is aimed at sites gaming the system, not ordinary service pages. Ranking noise still spikes around any big Google change, so check Search Console against 18-21 August before you rewrite anything.

What actually happened

Google's spam updates are separate from its better-known "core updates." Where a core update recalibrates how Google judges overall page quality and relevance, a spam update specifically hunts down sites using tactics that break Google's rules: things like AI-generated content built purely to game rankings, sites stuffed with auto-generated pages, or "reputation abuse" (piggybacking on a trusted domain's authority to rank unrelated junk pages).

This particular update ran quietly. Google logged it on its Search Status Dashboard, as it always does, but (as is now fairly typical for spam updates) didn't publish a blog post explaining what it targeted. It was the third spam update Google had run in 2026, following earlier ones in March and June.

Why this one felt rougher than normal

What made August's update stand out wasn't secrecy, it was scale. Ranking-tracking firm SE Ranking analysed 100,000 keywords across 20 industries in the US and found that during the update window, 16.71% of URLs that had been sitting in Google's top 10 fell out beyond position 100, effectively disappearing from page one entirely. In a typical fortnight, that figure sits closer to 9%. That's roughly an 82% jump in the rate of serious ranking losses compared with normal search volatility.

The disruption wasn't evenly spread. Sectors like fashion and beauty saw particularly high churn, while more transactional, trust-sensitive categories (finance, health, legal, the type Google calls "Your Money or Your Life" content) stayed comparatively steadier, which tracks with how carefully Google already scrutinises those niches. Alongside the losses, there was also a wave of new entrants: a noticeable share of URLs that hadn't previously cracked the top 20 suddenly appeared in the top 3, suggesting a genuine reshuffle rather than everyone simply dropping in unison.

Should you panic if your rankings dropped?

Not automatically, but it's worth checking, calmly. A spam update targets sites that are deliberately gaming the system, not ordinary small business websites with a normal mix of service pages, blog posts and contact details. If you've never mass-produced AI content, bought backlinks, or handed a subdomain over to an unrelated third party to publish on, a spam update is unlikely to be the direct cause of any drop you're seeing.

That said, two things are true at once here. First, general ranking volatility tends to spike around any major Google update, spam or otherwise. Sites can move for reasons only loosely connected to the update itself, simply because the wider results page is being reshuffled. Second, this is also a good moment to sense-check your own site with a critical eye, because some grey-area practices (an over-eager use of AI-written blog content with no editing, or an old backlink-buying campaign from a previous web developer) can look fine for months and then get caught in exactly this kind of enforcement wave.

What this means for your business

If you've noticed a ranking or traffic drop since late August, a sensible first step is a quick, honest audit rather than a guess:

  • Check Google Search Console's Performance report for the exact dates your clicks or impressions changed, and compare that to the 18-21 August window.
  • Look at which pages dropped. Is it site-wide, or concentrated on a specific batch of pages (for example, ones published in a rush, or written entirely by an AI tool with no human review)?
  • Review your backlink profile for anything that looks like it was bought or swapped rather than earned.
  • If nothing looks obviously wrong, sit tight for a few weeks. Search results often settle as an update fully rolls out and Google's systems recalibrate.

The broader lesson holds regardless of whether this particular update touched you: a website built on solid technical foundations, genuine content, and a clean backlink profile is inherently more resilient to this kind of volatility than one built on shortcuts. That's true whether the next update lands in a month or a year.

Frequently asked questions

Did Google's August 2026 update specifically target small business websites?

No. Spam updates target manipulative tactics (AI content farms, bought links, reputation abuse), not small business sites as a category. Most legitimate small business websites aren't the intended target.

How do I know if my site was affected by the spam update?

Check Search Console's Performance report for a drop specifically dated between 18 and 21 August 2026. A drop that starts and ends outside that window likely has a different cause.

What should I do if my rankings dropped after August 2026?

Start with a calm audit: check which pages dropped, review any AI-generated content for quality, and check your backlink profile. If nothing looks amiss, give it a few weeks to settle before making major changes.

Is every ranking drop caused by a Google update?

No. Competitors publishing new content, technical issues like slow load times or broken pages, and seasonal demand changes can all move rankings independently of any Google update.

A good moment for a website health check

Whether or not August's update touched your rankings, moments like this are a useful nudge to check your site's foundations are sound, from technical structure to how it's genuinely built for people, not just search engines. That's exactly the kind of review we cover in our SEO & GEO services, and if you've been putting off a proper look at your site, our free website design offer is a no-pressure way to see what a stronger foundation could look like, with no fee unless you decide to go ahead.

For more background on Google's recent moves, see our recent look at Google's August 2026 core update, and our guide to Google Search Console's key metrics if you want to dig into your own data.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review your Search Console data, check whether a drop is this update or something else, and decide what is worth changing.

item.title: Your YouTube Views Just Went Up. Here's Why That Doesn't Mean What You Think
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
If you post video on YouTube for your business and your view count suddenly looks healthier than usual, you have not gone viral. YouTube changed the definition of a "view" on 24 August 2026. Every video you have posted, and every one you post from now on, is being counted differently. It is a genuinely useful change once you understand it, but taken at face value it can make your video marketing look like it is performing better (or worse) than it actually is.

Key GLC Insight:

YouTube made the public view count bigger and left the commercial number where it always was. Judge videos on Engaged Views, watch time and retention in Studio, not the figure under the video.

What actually changed on 24 August

Before the update, YouTube counted views differently depending on format. Long-form videos needed a viewer to watch for several seconds, Shorts counted almost instantly, and live streams had their own rules. As of 24 August 2026, YouTube standardised this. A view now counts from the very first frame, across long-form, Shorts, podcasts and live content, including when a video autoplays in a feed. Simply seeing a thumbnail still does not count, but a thumbnail that triggers autoplay now does.

YouTube said the change was about ending "metric confusion". Creators and businesses posting across formats were comparing numbers that were never really comparable. That is a fair problem to want to fix. The side effect, which YouTube has acknowledged openly, is that public view counts are going up, noticeably. Early analysis from ad-tech firm Agentio estimates long-form view counts are running around 30% higher than before, and Shorts view counts as much as 65% higher, simply because of how the count now starts.

Views vs Engaged Views: the number that actually matters

To keep things honest, YouTube renamed its old, stricter counting method "Engaged Views". This is what happens when someone actually clicks to watch, or keeps watching past the first few seconds. Engaged Views is still what YouTube uses for the numbers that matter commercially. Monetisation eligibility under the Partner Programme, and the core analytics (average view duration, click-through rate and retention) are all still built on it, not the new headline count.

In other words, YouTube gave everyone a bigger public number and quietly kept the real one where it has always been, in YouTube Studio under Analytics, Advanced Mode. If you only ever look at the number under your video, you are now looking at the wrong one.

What this means for your business

If you use YouTube for your business (product demos, how-to content, local advertising, or brand-building), here is the practical bit:

  • Do not compare before-and-after. A video posted in July and one posted in September are not measured the same way any more, so a jump in views around late August tells you nothing about whether your content actually improved.
  • Ignore the headline number when judging performance. Use Engaged Views, average view duration and retention in Analytics if you want to know whether people are genuinely interested, not just whether they were shown a thumbnail that autoplayed.
  • If you run YouTube ads, ask what you are being billed or benchmarked on. Anyone quoting you view-based pricing or "look how many views your last video got" should be specific about which number they mean. Public views and engaged views are no longer the same thing.
  • Your earnings and monetisation status are unaffected, so there is no action needed there. This is purely a reporting and perception change.

This is really a subset of a bigger pattern we keep coming back to on this blog. Platforms regularly change how they measure things, and the businesses that get caught out are the ones making decisions off a single headline metric instead of understanding what is actually being counted. It is the same lesson as reading Google Search Console properly rather than trusting a dashboard number at face value, and it sits alongside how we think about SEO and GEO measurement on your website.

Where this fits with paid media

If part of your marketing budget goes towards YouTube or Google video advertising, this is worth raising with whoever manages that spend. Reporting built around vanity metrics can quietly drift away from reporting that reflects actual return on ad spend. It is one of the reasons our own paid media work is built around reporting clients can act on, not just numbers that look impressive in a screenshot. The same caution applies as newer discovery channels pick up ads, which we covered in our guide to ChatGPT ads for UK advertisers.

Frequently asked questions

Does the YouTube view count change affect monetisation or earnings?

No. YouTube has confirmed that the Partner Programme and monetisation eligibility are still based on Engaged Views, not the new headline view count, so nothing changes there.

Where do I find my real Engaged Views number in YouTube Analytics?

In YouTube Studio, go to Analytics and switch to Advanced Mode. Engaged Views and the older, stricter counting method are shown there alongside the new headline view count.

Will my old videos' view counts change retroactively?

Yes, the counting method applies platform-wide, so historic videos will show higher public view counts than before, even though nothing about the video itself changed.

Should I change my video marketing strategy because of this?

Not because of the counting change itself. It is a good moment to start judging your videos by engaged views, watch time and retention rather than the public number, but the underlying content and strategy questions have not changed.

A quick, honest next step

None of this requires an overhaul, just a slightly more careful eye on which number you are looking at. But if this has you wondering whether your website and wider digital presence are being measured, tracked and reported on properly at all, that is exactly the kind of thing worth a second look. Our free website design offer is a no-obligation way to get a professional set of eyes on where you stand, with no pressure to go any further if it is not for you.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review how your video, search and paid reporting is actually being counted, and what is worth acting on.

item.title: Threads Just Removed Link-Click Tracking. Here's How to Measure Your Traffic Anyway
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
On 8 September 2026, Meta rolled out a big redesign of the Insights panel inside Threads. There are now AI-generated summaries that tell you whether a post did better, worse or typical compared with your recent history, plus new breakdowns of which communities are driving your engagement and how much of your reach comes from followers versus people discovering you fresh.

Key GLC Insight:

Threads Insights can tell you a post resonated. It can no longer tell you whether anyone visited your site. Tag your links and measure the click on your website, not inside the app.

Sounds like an upgrade, and in some ways it is. But buried in the same update is something that matters a lot more if you use Threads to send people to your website. Link-click data has been removed from the analytics entirely. If you post a link to a product page, a blog post or a booking form, Threads will now tell you plenty about likes, reposts and audience mix, and nothing at all about whether anyone actually clicked through.

What Threads actually changed

Threads chief Connor Hayes described the update as helping creators "see how each post did and what actually drove the results", with new metrics on audience reach and how much of it is followers versus new viewers. That is a genuine improvement for anyone using Threads to build a following.

What Meta has not explained is why link clicks disappeared. A spokesperson told Engadget the company was "exploring" the feature but would not say more, and there is no confirmed date for when click data actually stopped appearing. It seems to have quietly gone missing before the wider redesign was announced. It fits a pattern Meta has followed for a while. Threads has long been suspected of downranking posts that contain outbound links, and removing the one metric that shows those links working is consistent with a platform that would rather keep people scrolling inside the app than send them elsewhere.

Why this matters if you post links to promote your business

If you have been using Threads to drive traffic and judging success by the in-app numbers, you have just lost your only feedback loop. You can see a post got 40 reposts and assume it is working, but you have no way of knowing from Threads itself whether that translated into a single visit to your site, let alone an enquiry or a sale.

This is not unique to Threads. Plenty of platforms are gradually reporting less about what happens after someone leaves their app, because their business model rewards keeping attention in-house rather than handing it off to yours. YouTube recently made a similar move when it changed how views are counted, which we unpacked in our post on the YouTube view count change in 2026. The lesson is not to stop using Threads. It is that you cannot rely on any single platform to tell you honestly whether it is working for you. That job has to sit with your own website.

What this means for your business

If your marketing includes posting links on Threads (or Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn or anywhere else), you need to be measuring the click on your side, not theirs. In practice that means three things:

  1. Tag every link you share. Adding simple tracking tags (called UTM parameters) to any link you post tells your own analytics exactly which platform, post or campaign sent a visitor, regardless of what that platform chooses to report.
  2. Have analytics actually set up on your website. This sounds obvious, but a surprising number of small business sites either have no analytics installed, or have it installed incorrectly, so even a well-tagged link goes nowhere useful.
  3. Look at your own numbers, not platform vanity metrics. Reposts and likes tell you a post resonated. Only your website analytics can tell you whether it made you any money.

None of this requires becoming a data analyst. It requires your website being set up properly in the first place, something that should happen automatically when a site is built, not bolted on later as an afterthought.

How to track link clicks from Threads

The practical fix is straightforward. Before you post a link on Threads (or any social platform), add UTM parameters to it. Free tools exist to generate these in seconds, so the link records which platform and post it came from. Then make sure Google Analytics and Google Search Console are properly connected to your site, so those tagged visits show up as real data you can act on rather than guesswork. If you want a step-by-step on the Search Console side, we covered getting Search Console set up and which metrics actually matter in an earlier post.

If you are running paid social or search campaigns alongside your organic posting, this is exactly the kind of spend-to-enquiry tracking we build in from day one for paid media clients, because a platform's own reporting is never the full picture.

Frequently asked questions

Does Threads show link click data any more?

No. As of the September 2026 Insights redesign, Threads no longer reports link clicks anywhere in its analytics, even though it now shows more detail on views, reach and audience makeup.

How do I track link clicks from Threads to my website?

Add UTM parameters to any link before you post it, then check the results in Google Analytics rather than relying on the platform's own numbers.

What are UTM parameters and do I need them?

They are small tags added to the end of a URL that tell your website analytics where a visitor came from. If you post links on any social platform, they are worth using every time.

Is Threads still worth using for my small business?

That depends on your goals. It can still be useful for visibility and audience building, but you should no longer expect it to tell you whether it is driving business results. That measurement now has to happen on your own site.

An easy first step

If reading this made you realise you are not actually sure what your website's analytics are set up to track (or whether they are set up at all), that is worth sorting before you spend more time posting links anywhere. Every website we build comes with Google Search Console and Google Analytics configured properly from the start, so you can see what is really happening rather than hoping for the best.

We currently have a free website offer running with no obligation, a good, low-risk way to find out what a properly built site with proper tracking looks like.

item.title: Google Just Auto-Upgraded Your Search Ads to AI Max. Here's What Small Businesses Need to Check
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
If you run Google Ads for your business and you noticed something looking different in your account this month, you are not imagining it. Since 1 September 2026, Google has been automatically migrating any Search campaign still using campaign-level broad match or automatically created assets over to its newer AI Max system. The Google Ads AI Max upgrade runs through the end of September, and unlike most Google Ads changes, there is no way to opt out of it.

Key GLC Insight:

Google is moving Search campaigns onto AI Max through the end of September, with no opt-out. Check when yours moved, tighten negatives and daily caps, and confirm your live ads still sound like your business.

What the Google Ads AI Max upgrade is actually changing

AI Max is not a new feature you will be offered. It is Google folding several older, more manual settings into one AI-managed system that decides which search terms your ads show for and, in some cases, rewrites your ad headlines and descriptions on the fly. Google quietly stopped letting anyone create new campaigns with the old settings back in early August, and from 1 to 30 September it is converting existing campaigns in place, a few at a time rather than all in one go.

The detail worth knowing is this. Campaigns that only had broad match switched on are being migrated with the automatic headline and description rewriting turned off, while campaigns that were using Google's automatically created assets are being migrated with that rewriting turned on. Search term matching, which is the part of AI Max that decides how loosely your ads match what someone actually typed, is being switched on for everyone. If you have never dug into your Google Ads settings before, none of this will mean much on its own. What matters is the effect it can have on your account.

Google says it is designing the migration to be as smooth as possible, and for a lot of accounts it probably will be. But independent testing reported by industry publications has found AI Max campaigns picking up noticeably more invalid or low-quality clicks than the older match types, and lower returns on ad spend in some comparisons. That is not a reason to panic. It is a reason to check your account rather than assume nothing has changed.

Why this hits a small budget harder than a big one

A large advertiser spending tens of thousands of pounds a month can usually absorb a handful of low-quality clicks without noticing. A local business spending a few hundred pounds a month on Google Ads cannot. When search term matching is loosened, your ads can start showing for searches that are only loosely related to what you actually offer. On a small daily budget, even a short run of expensive, off-target clicks can eat a real share of your spend before you have spotted it.

This is exactly the kind of thing GLC watches for clients running Google Ads campaigns, because attribution and spend efficiency matter more, not less, when the budget is tight.

What this means for your business

If you or someone on your team manages your own Google Ads account, it is worth ten minutes this month to check a few things:

  • Look for a recent change to your Search campaigns. Google has added new reporting fields that show exactly when a campaign was migrated, so you can compare performance before and after the switch.
  • Check your negative keyword lists. These become more important under AI Max, not less, because they are one of your few remaining ways to tell Google what you do not want to show up for.
  • Review your daily budget caps, especially if you are running on a tight monthly spend. A lower daily cap limits how much a bad few days can cost you while you watch how the new settings behave.
  • Check your ad headlines and descriptions if you were using automatically created assets. Google can now rewrite these automatically, so it is worth confirming what is actually live still sounds like your business.

If you do not manage your own account, or you have never been entirely sure what broad match even means, that is a normal position to be in. It is also exactly the kind of change that is easy to miss until a monthly bill looks higher than expected for no obvious reason.

Frequently asked questions

What is Google Ads AI Max?

It is Google's newer, AI-driven system for managing Search campaign targeting and ad creative, replacing the older broad match and automatically created assets settings. The Google Ads AI Max upgrade is the September 2026 migration of those older settings onto that system.

Did Google change my Google Ads campaign without asking me?

If your Search campaigns were using campaign-level broad match or automatically created assets, Google began migrating them automatically from 1 September 2026. You were not asked campaign by campaign.

Can I opt out of the AI Max upgrade?

No. Google has removed the option to keep the old settings. The only choice available is whether you configure the migration yourself in advance or let Google's default settings apply.

Will AI Max make my Google Ads more expensive?

Not necessarily, but broader search term matching can bring in lower-quality clicks on some accounts, which can push up cost per genuine enquiry if it is not monitored. Checking performance before and after your migration date is the way to find out.

Not sure what is happening in your own Google Ads account?

This is a genuinely small change to explain and a genuinely easy one to miss if you are busy running the actual business rather than reading Google's release notes. If you would rather have someone keep an eye on this kind of thing for you, GLC's paid marketing service covers Google Ads and Meta Ads setup and ongoing management, with attribution that connects your spend to real enquiries rather than vanity clicks. For a related read, we covered ChatGPT Ads for UK advertisers if you are weighing up where else your ad budget could go.

And if this has you wondering whether your website itself is doing its job, not just your ads, our free website design offer is a no-obligation way to find out. You see a professional design first and only pay if you are happy to proceed.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to review your Google Ads account after the AI Max migration, and to check whether your spend is still going on the searches you actually want.

item.title: Facebook Just Started Charging Small Businesses to Link to Their Own Website
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
Facebook charging for link posts is no longer a rumour buried in a help document. If you run a Facebook Page for your business, you may have noticed something new this month. Meta is limiting how many posts with links you can publish for free. As of this week, non-paying Facebook Pages are capped at two link posts a month. Want to post more links to your website, your booking page or a blog update? Meta wants you to pay for a Meta One for Business subscription to do it.

Key GLC Insight:

Facebook charging for link posts is the till, not the news. Organic reach on rented platforms has been shrinking for years. Pay for the click, or send people to a website you own.

This is rolling out now, on the back of a similar restriction Meta first trialled in December 2025, and it is worth five minutes of your time to understand, whether or not it ends up affecting your Page.

What actually changed

Meta One for Business launched this month with four paid tiers, priced in US dollars where it has been observed so far. Meta has not confirmed UK pricing or a full UK rollout yet. The free tier gives you two link posts (or link comments) a month across Facebook. If you want more, the tiers run from around $15 a month for Basic, still capped at two links but with other perks, up to around $500 a month for Premium, which removes the Facebook link cap entirely and allows up to 12 Instagram Reel links a month.

A few things are exempt from the count, so they are worth knowing if you post regularly:

  • Links added as a comment under a post that already has one
  • Links to Meta's own platforms (Instagram, WhatsApp, Threads)
  • Facebook affiliate links
  • Any link inside a paid advert
  • Publisher Pages, the news and media accounts Meta relies on for content, which are exempt entirely

Why Meta is doing this now

It is tempting to read this as Meta squeezing small businesses for cash, and there is certainly an element of that. But Meta's own data gives useful context. By its own reporting, external links made up under 2% of what people actually saw in their feeds during the first quarter of 2026, down from close to 10% back in 2022. The algorithm has been quietly burying link posts in favour of native content (video, photos, text updates) for years. This change does not really take anything away from most Pages. It monetises a habit Facebook had already made close to pointless.

That is the real story here, and it is one GLC has been saying for a while. Organic reach on rented platforms has been shrinking steadily, and this is just the next visible step.

What this means for your business

If you are a sole trader or small business that occasionally shares a link to a new blog post, a special offer or a booking page on your Facebook Page, two things are worth checking now.

First, work out whether your account is actually in the affected group. Meta has described this as a limited, region-by-region test, so it may not have reached your Page yet, and it is not worth paying for a tier you do not need before you have confirmed you are restricted.

Second, and more importantly, do not treat this as a Facebook problem to solve with a Facebook subscription. If two free links a month feels tight, that is a sign your business is leaning too heavily on a platform you do not own and cannot control the rules of. The exemption for adverts is telling. Meta is happy for you to link to your site all you like, as long as you are paying to promote the post. Organic traffic is being nudged towards the checkout.

For local service businesses in particular (dog walkers, tradespeople, coaches, anyone who posts regularly to keep their community updated) this is a reminder that Facebook should be one channel feeding people back to a website you control, not the only place your business exists online. We wrote about that in more detail for website design for dog walkers, and the same idea applies to any local trade. We touched on a similar theme when Threads quietly removed link click tracking a few weeks ago. Platforms keep changing the rules on the traffic you send them, but they cannot touch the traffic that already lands on your own site through search or a well-run ad campaign.

What to do about Facebook charging for link posts

A few practical steps if this affects you:

  • Check your Page's posting tools for a link post counter before you assume you are restricted.
  • If you do hit the limit, save your two free links a month for the posts that matter most, a big offer or a genuine announcement, rather than routine updates.
  • Consider whether a small, well-targeted Meta ad budget makes more sense than an ongoing Meta One subscription. Adverts are not capped, and unlike a subscription, ad spend is directly tied to reach you can measure. That is the kind of measured spend we build into our Google and Meta ads service.
  • Longer term, make sure your website itself is doing the job of converting visitors, not just Facebook. A page that ranks well in Google search and converts on arrival needs Facebook a lot less.

Frequently asked questions

Is Facebook charging for link posts on every Page?

Not necessarily. Every professional Page gets two free link posts a month. You only need Meta One for Business if you regularly post more than that, and only if the cap has reached your Page.

Does this affect Facebook ads?

No. Links inside paid adverts are exempt from the count entirely, along with links to other Meta apps like Instagram and WhatsApp.

Is this rolled out everywhere yet?

Not confirmed as global. Meta has described it as a limited test expanding from a December 2025 trial, so check your own Page's posting tools rather than assuming you are affected. UK pricing has not been confirmed either.

Should I just stop using Facebook for my business?

No, but this is a good prompt to check your website is doing the heavy lifting, not your Facebook Page. Facebook is still useful for community and visibility. It should not be the only place people can find or contact your business.

An easy first step

Changes like this land on our desk every week, which is exactly why we keep an eye on them so you do not have to. If this has made you wonder whether your own website is pulling its weight, we will design you a free website with no obligation to go further so you can see what a site built to convert, not just exist, actually looks like. Every website we build is set up to be found in search and to convert on arrival, so Facebook becomes one useful channel rather than the only place your business lives.

And if paid social is part of your plan, our Google and Meta ads service is built to make sure that spend is measured properly, not just guessed at.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions to check whether your website is doing the heavy lifting, or whether you are still renting your whole online presence from Facebook.

item.title: WordPress 7.1.1: The Security Update You Can't Ignore
item.dc:creator: Gareth Cross
item.content:encoded:
On 18 September 2026, WordPress released version 7.1.1. This WordPress security update September 2026 patches 11 separate vulnerabilities in the software that runs a huge share of the world's websites, including, in all likelihood, your own. The headline fix is a bug hiding in blog comments. If you have never thought about which version of WordPress your site is running, this is a good week to start.

Key GLC Insight:

Comment moderation is a workflow step, not a security control. If nobody is applying WordPress core, plugin and theme patches, a queue of unpublished comments will not keep a site safe.

What actually happened

WordPress 7.1.1 fixes 11 security issues at once, which is a lot for a single point release. The one worth understanding is a stored cross-site scripting flaw, catalogued as CVE-2026-93485, hiding inside a core function called wpautop(). That function runs on almost every piece of content your site displays, turning line breaks into paragraphs. The bug means an attacker could sneak malicious code into a page through something as ordinary as a blog comment, without needing a login of any kind.

Comments on most sites sit in a moderation queue before they go live, so this is not quite as alarming as it sounds at first glance. But as the official WordPress announcement itself pointed out, moderation is a workflow step, not a security control, and it should not be relied on as one. The other 10 fixes in the release are lower severity and mostly need some level of existing account access to exploit, covering things like unauthorised post overwrites and draft content being exposed.

What this means for your business

If your website runs on WordPress, which a very large share of small business sites do, this update applies to you whether you built the site yourself, had a freelancer put it together, or it has been quietly running in the background for years without anyone giving it much thought. A handful of specific situations are worth paying attention to:

  • If your host or developer manages updates for you, this has probably already been handled. Worth a quick email to confirm rather than assuming.
  • If you or a member of staff logs into WordPress to update the site yourselves, you will want to check the version number is 7.1.1 (or the relevant patched version if you are on an older major release).
  • If nobody has updated the site in months, this is a useful nudge to check what else might have been missed alongside it. Security releases rarely arrive on their own. Plugins and themes need the same attention.

None of this needs to be a fire drill. WordPress ships security fixes several times a year, and for most sites the sensible response is a calm, five-minute check rather than a scramble.

Do you need to do anything?

For sites with automatic background updates switched on, which is the WordPress default for minor and security releases, the WordPress security update September 2026 should already be rolling out on its own. For everything else, it is a manual job. Log in to the WordPress dashboard, go to Updates, and apply the patch if it has not already installed itself.

If your site was custom-built with heavy modifications to core files (rare, but it happens), it is worth a quick check with whoever built it before updating, just to be safe. For the overwhelming majority of small business sites, though, this is a routine, low-risk update.

How to stay on top of this without becoming a part-time sysadmin

This is exactly the kind of thing that is easy to let slide when you are busy running an actual business rather than a website. A few habits make it far less likely to catch you out:

  • Turn on automatic updates for WordPress core, and for any plugin you trust, if you have not already.
  • Keep a short list of what plugins and themes are installed, so a security bulletin like this one is quick to check against.
  • If checking and applying updates is not something you want on your own plate, it is a reasonable thing to hand to whoever manages your hosting.

At GLC, sites we build come with SSL and the security basics set up from day one, and we also offer an ongoing managed service (details on our costs page) that includes keeping an eye on exactly this kind of update, so it is one less thing on your list. More on how we approach builds and ongoing support is on our website design and development page. We have also previously rounded up the best WordPress security plugins worth layering on top of core updates like this one.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if my WordPress site updated automatically?

Log in to your WordPress dashboard and open Updates, or look at the version number shown at the bottom of most admin screens. If it reads 7.1.1 (or your relevant patched branch), you are covered.

Is it safe to turn on automatic WordPress updates?

For core security releases like this one, yes, and it is the setting WordPress recommends by default. Automatic updates for plugins and themes are usually safe too, though it is sensible to keep backups running in case any individual plugin update causes a conflict.

What happens if I do not update WordPress?

Your site keeps working exactly as before, at least for now. But it stays exposed to whichever vulnerabilities the update fixed, and unpatched WordPress sites are a common target for automated attacks that scan the web looking for exactly this kind of gap.

How often should a WordPress website be updated?

Core security releases like this one should be applied as soon as they are available, ideally automatically. Plugins and themes are worth checking at least monthly, alongside a working backup.

If this has you wondering about your own site

If reading this made you realise you are not entirely sure who is responsible for keeping your website patched and secure, that is a completely normal thing to not know, and an easy thing to fix. Our free website design offer is a no-obligation way to get a second pair of eyes on where your site currently stands, security included.

Contact Gareth at GLC Web Solutions if you want a straight answer on whether your WordPress site is actually being kept up to date.
